author: Nelev
body:
21 tests covering the two pieces of the frontend that carry logic, plus a `ui` workflow so any of it actually runs on a PR — there was only `api.yml` before, so `medas-ui` had no automated check at all.

## Tooling

Vitest + React Testing Library, per Next's own testing guide. That guide recommends E2E over unit tests for `async` Server Components, which puts `app/page.tsx` out of scope here.

## What is covered

**`api/chat.ts`** — stubs `globalThis.fetch` rather than mocking the module, so URL building and response mapping actually run. Every bug this file has had lived in exactly those two places: a `fetch("")`, a `//conversations` double slash, a `{ message }` wrapper the API answers with a 422, and a declared return type that did not match what the server sends.

**`ChatComposer`** — mocks the API client instead, since its contract with the server is covered above. What matters at this level is which of the two calls the composer picks (create vs append), and what it does with the answer.

## Two things worth a look in review

**The tests were mutation-checked, not just run.** Breaking `api/chat.ts` failed the right test. But breaking the composer — appending the create response instead of replacing with it — initially passed all 21, because with an empty store `[...messages, ...created.messages]` is identical to `created.messages`. That assertion was asserting nothing. It now seeds a stale message so the two are distinguishable, and the mutation fails as it should.

**Two tests pin a defect rather than hiding it.** `handleSubmit` has no `catch`, so a failed send is silent to the user and the rejection escapes to the runner, failing the whole run with exit 1 even when every assertion passes. The suppression is scoped to those two tests, so a stray rejection anywhere else still fails the suite. The test named *"does not tell the user anything went wrong"* says in a comment to delete it once the handler surfaces an error.

## Notes

- `test/setup.ts` resets the zustand store before each test — it is a module singleton, so without that, whichever test ran first would decide the next one's result.
- API response shapes live in `test/fixtures.ts`, so a contract change is a one-file edit.
- Vite 5 resolves tsconfig paths natively, so `vite-tsconfig-paths` was dropped after it warned it was redundant.
- In the workflow, `corepack enable` comes **before** `setup-node`: `cache: yarn` asks yarn where its cache lives, and without corepack that question reaches the Yarn 1 the runner ships rather than the Yarn 4 pinned in `package.json`.
